item.title: Supercurrent enables the reading of quantum information without destroying it
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article reports a new technique that uses a supercurrent to perform a quantum‑non‑demolition readout of a qubit, allowing the state to be inferred without causing collapse. By leveraging dissipation‑free superconducting currents, the method sidesteps the trade‑off between measurement fidelity and back‑action that has limited many superconducting processors, complementing recent progress in dispersive readout and error‑corrected logical qubits. If scalable, such nondestructive sensing could simplify syndrome extraction in surface‑code architectures and reduce overhead for quantum error correction, though integration with existing control hardware remains an open challenge.

One of the fundamental challenges of quantum computing is obtaining information from a quantum bit, or qubit. Unlike a conventional bit, which can be read repeatedly without altering its content, direct measurement of a quantum system typically causes the state to collapse before it can be determined. In other words, reading the information modifies it.

item.title: Maximal Orbital Entanglement from Non-Interacting Fermions
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that even the simplest mean‑field states—Slater determinants of non‑interacting fermions—can saturate the theoretical limit of orbital entanglement for a wide range of particle numbers and lattice sizes, overturning the common belief that free‑fermion wavefunctions are useless as quantum resources. By proving closed‑form bounds on total correlation across arbitrary bipartitions, the work bridges many‑body simulation techniques with quantum information theory, suggesting that existing electronic‑structure codes could be repurposed to generate highly entangled registers for near‑term quantum processors. The result opens a practical pathway to harvest entanglement from readily preparable states, though exploiting it will still require careful orbital rotations and error‑robust encoding schemes.

Orbital rotations are used in quantum many-body physics and chemistry to reduce the complexity of quantum states by compressing their correlation into a small set of relevant orbitals. In striking contrast, quantum information processing strives for the opposite: orbitals that maximize entanglement as a resource. Motivated by this, we prove that Slater determinants of $N$ fermions on a lattice of $d_A + d_B = d$ sites, although free of particle correlation, can carry up to $\min\{d_A, d_B, N, d-N\}$ ebits of orbital entanglement. Given enough particles and holes, this equals the maximum over all fermionic states. For arbitrary free states, we derive the maximal orbital total correlation in closed form for all bipartitions, the finest partition, and all partitions of up to five sites, using new majorization relations for Hermitian matrices. Taken together, these results turn mean-field states, the starting point of most many-body methods in physics and chemistry, into a viable resource for quantum information processing.

item.title: Distributed Quantum-Centric Supercomputing with Multi-Layered Generative Learning for Intermolecular Interactions
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how a distributed quantum‑centric supercomputing framework can break large electronic‑structure problems into smaller fragments that fit on near‑term quantum processors, dramatically cutting qubit counts, circuit depth and sampling cost while still capturing inter‑fragment correlations through a clever two‑step aggregation scheme. By pairing the physics‑informed generative SQD solver with an additional generative model to identify the most important sectors of Hilbert space, the authors achieve up to a 95 % reduction in diagonalization size for water and formamide dimers—an advance that dovetails with recent fragment‑based VQE and quantum embedding efforts. If the approach scales to bigger molecules, it could make high‑accuracy quantum chemistry simulations feasible on today’s hybrid HPC‑quantum platforms, though the overall workflow still relies on substantial classical post‑processing and careful error mitigation.

Quantum-centric supercomputing (QCSC) approaches, such as sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), combine quantum processors with high-performance computers (HPC), offering a promising route toward solving challenging electronic structure problems. However, implementation of QCSC approaches to large active space calculations is constrained by the associated number of qubits, deep quantum circuits, sampling cost, and large-scale Hamiltonian diagonalization. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a distributed QCSC framework that decomposes complex molecular problems into parallel sub-problems requiring fewer qubits, shallower circuits, and reduced shot budgets. A physically motivated, two-step aggregation scheme then reconstructs the global solution: first, a computational bit assignment strategy optimizes a cost function to appropriately map local bit indices to global ones, yielding a mapped tensor product state (MTPS); second, an inter-fragment correlation recovery module restores missing cross-fragment interactions. Herein, we employ a multi-layered generative machine learning architecture, starting with utilizing the recently proposed physics-informed generative SQD (PIGen-SQD) as a distributed QCSC solver, followed by a secondary generative module to model configuration distributions and identify dominant sectors of the global Hilbert space. For water and formamide dimers, our method achieves up to $95\%$ reduction in the diagonalization dimension while enhancing energy accuracy by an order of magnitude over conventional SQD. Furthermore, application to the water hexamer ($\mathrm{(H_2O)_6}$) cage successfully decomposes a 120-qubit problem into six 20-qubit monomeric subsystems, and stitches the monomers under a dimeric approximation, demonstrating excellent agreement with the reference classical methods.

item.title: Generating entanglement in quantum matter with pathway-entangled photons via resonant inelastic X-ray scattering
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how resonant inelastic X‑ray scattering can be turned from a passive probe into an active source of heralded entanglement between distant regions of a solid, essentially bringing the DLCZ quantum‑network recipe into the hard‑X‑ray regime. By demonstrating that pathway‑entangled photons can project a material onto maximally entangled edge excitations—whether simple two‑site Bell pairs or fractionalized spins in an AKLT chain—the work opens a new route for linking quantum‑matter platforms to photonic quantum information processing. The proposal is timely because it leverages emerging X‑ray interferometry and ultrafast detectors, but its practical impact will hinge on achieving sufficient phase stability and photon‑count rates in realistic scattering experiments.

Resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) is conventionally used to probe elementary excitations and correlations in quantum materials. Here, we propose an interferometric RIXS protocol that instead creates entanglement between spatially separated regions of a solid-state material. An incident X-ray photon is coherently split by a beam splitter into two arms illuminating opposite ends of a sample. Recombining the scattered photons at a second beam splitter and detecting an energy-selected photon then projects the material into a coherent superposition of excitations at the two ends. This protocol is the X-ray, solid-state analogue of the Duan-Lukin-Cirac-Zoller (DLCZ) heralding scheme. Using a Kramers-Heisenberg formalism with quantized photon modes, we show that orthogonal and degenerate end excitations yield maximally entangled states. We illustrate this mechanism in three models: (1) two decoupled sites yield a heralded Bell state. (2) An open tight-binding chain exhibits reflection-parity-dependent interference, providing a benchmark for the interferometer's coherence. (3) A spin-1 Haldane (AKLT) chain yields an entangled pair of fractionalized edge spins. We also discuss practical considerations and challenges for realizing the protocol in X-ray experiments.

item.title: One-sided-DIQKD using any pure bipartite entangled state secure against all attacks
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that one‑sided‑device‑independent QKD can be made secure with any pure bipartite entangled state, eliminating the need for costly maximally‑entangled resources and expanding the usable regime to nearly separable states. By linking security directly to quantum steering rather than full Bell nonlocality, it aligns with recent efforts to relax device‑trust assumptions while still protecting against all attacks, a step forward from earlier qubit‑only, fully‑device‑independent schemes. The practical upshot is that existing telecom‑grade sources and detectors could already support robust key generation in realistic networks, though the required detection efficiencies and visibilities must still meet the thresholds identified for each state.

Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) allows spatially separated parties to establish a secret key among themselves based on quantum principles. While QKD systems are being deployed worldwide, their reliance on trusted measurements makes them vulnerable. Moreover, existing protocols have largely focussed on the qubit cases, and rely on the maximally entangled state, a costly resource to generate. Here, we consider the one-sided-device-independent (1SDI) QKD protocols, where one of the measurement devices is trusted while the other is untrusted. The resource in this scenario is quantum steering, an asymmetric form of quantum nonlocality. This is inspired by a real-world scenario, where the trusted party can be considered to be a bank, or any large organisation that has sufficient resources to protect its systems and validate them, while the users are vulnerable to attacks. We then demonstrate that a secure key can be obtained using any pure bipartite entangled state in this setup. Considering realistic detectors and sources based on current technology, we demonstrate that even states that are almost separable can be used to extract a secure key. Moreover, for every pure entangled bipartite state, we find the critical detection efficiencies and visibility to obtain a secure key.

item.title: Fermion Scattering on Quantum Computers
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks one of the first concrete demonstrations that a hybrid qubit‑qumode processor can simulate real‑time fermion–antifermion scattering and resolve resonance formation in a (1+1)‑dimensional Yukawa model, providing a practical benchmark for near‑term quantum hardware. By combining digital encoding of fermions with continuous‑variable representation of the scalar field, the authors bridge the gap between abstract quantum‑field‑theory algorithms and experimentally accessible photonic platforms, complementing recent tensor‑network studies of low‑dimensional QFT dynamics. The ability to extract decay rates and Breit–Wigner resonance profiles with percent‑level accuracy shows that local observables on hybrid devices can already probe nontrivial particle physics phenomena, though scaling to higher dimensions and larger lattices will still demand significant advances in error mitigation and hardware connectivity.

Resonant scattering links particle interactions to the formation and decay of unstable excitations. We develop a hybrid quantum-computing framework to study these dynamics through fermion--antifermion collisions. Our formulation of $(1+1)$-dimensional Yukawa theory encodes fermions in qubits and the scalar field in qumodes. We identify the operations needed for a photonic implementation and benchmark the dynamics with tensor-network simulations. Near resonance, we resolve the build-up of a localised scalar excitation and the subsequent partial return of energy to the fermions. Enhanced entanglement accompanies this exchange. Time-dependent correlator measurements reproduce the analytically predicted decay rate to a few percent precision, with energy scans exhibiting a resonance peak consistent with packet-averaged Breit--Wigner behaviour. These results establish a concrete scattering benchmark for hybrid quantum computers and demonstrate how local real-time observables can probe particle-resonance dynamics.

item.title: Hardware-Friendly Estimation of LCU-Based Expectation Values via Quantum-to-Classical Workload Shifting
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces HERMES, a method that shifts the entire linear‑combination‑of‑unitaries (LCU) processing from quantum hardware to classical post‑processing, eliminating ancilla qubits, controlled unitaries and the explosion of circuit repetitions that have limited LCU techniques on NISQ and early fault‑tolerant devices. By expanding both the operator and observable in the Pauli basis and using a two‑level measurement‑reduction scheme, HERMES keeps the number of distinct measurement settings fixed while still delivering accurate expectation values, a practical advance over recent randomized LCU approaches that scale linearly with sample count. The demonstrated performance on H₂ and LiH ground‑state energy estimation shows that shallow, gate‑light circuits can now be leveraged for variational simulations without the heavy hardware overhead previously assumed necessary. If the classical sampling overhead remains manageable, this could broaden the applicability of LCU‑based algorithms across chemistry, sensing and beyond.

Estimating the expectation value of an observable $O$ for a quantum state evolved under a general, possibly non-unitary, operator $A$ is a fundamental task in quantum simulation, chemistry, and variational algorithms. Existing linear-combination-of-unitaries (LCU) approaches implement $A$ on hardware, requiring ancilla qubits, controlled unitaries and, in randomized variants, fresh circuit executions for every Monte Carlo sample. These costs are prohibitive on NISQ and early fault-tolerant devices. We propose HERMES (Hardware-Efficient Reusable Measurements for Estimating LCU-based expectation valueS), which moves the processing of $A$ entirely to the classical domain. Expanding $A$ and $O$ in the Pauli basis and sampling pairs of Pauli terms classically, HERMES rewrites $μ= \mathrm{Tr}(OAρA^{\dagger})/\mathrm{Tr}(AρA^{\dagger})$ as a ratio of weighted sums of Pauli expectation values on the unmodified state $ρ$, with no ancillas, controlled unitaries, or quantum implementation of $A$. A two-level measurement reduction scheme (Pauli deduplication and commuting-group partitioning) bounds the number of distinct measurement settings independently of the sample count, unlike randomized LCU methods whose circuit executions grow linearly with it. On ground-state energy estimation of $\mathrm{H}_2$ and $\mathrm{LiH}$ via imaginary-time evolution, HERMES matches or beats Pauli single-ancilla LCU baseline using shallow circuits with no two-qubit gates beyond state preparation under qubit-wise commuting grouping. It is also more robust to noise and completes a noisy $\mathrm{LiH}$ simulation infeasible for the baseline, at the cost of classical overhead growing with the number of Pauli terms in $A$.

item.title: Quantum Machine Learning in Medical Imaging: A Primer for Radiologists
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it translates the abstract promise of quantum machine learning into concrete language that radiologists can actually grasp, highlighting how NISQ‑era hardware could one day alleviate the massive compute demands of modern deep‑learning pipelines. By cataloguing existing hybrid quantum‑classical approaches—such as variational circuits and quantum image encodings—and showing early results on tasks like tumor classification, it situates quantum methods within the broader push toward more efficient medical imaging analytics while making clear that current demonstrations are limited to tiny datasets and simulators. The review therefore serves both as a realistic checkpoint for clinicians curious about quantum acceleration and as a roadmap for researchers aiming to move these prototypes toward clinically viable scale.

Deep learning has transformed radiology, but the computational cost of training and deploying modern models is outpacing what classical hardware can support. Quantum computing has been proposed as one response to this bottleneck: an n-qubit system can represent $2^n$ states simultaneously, although practical speedups require efficient algorithms, data encoding, and measurement strategies rather than superposition alone. This review introduces radiologists to five core quantum concepts, qubits, superposition, entanglement, quantum gates, and quantum circuits, and to the superconducting, trapped-ion, and photonic hardware platforms that define the current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era. We then summarize the quantum machine learning architectures most often applied to medical imaging (quantum support vector machines, quantum neural networks, variational quantum circuits, and quantum convolutional neural networks) and quantum image representations such as the flexible representation of quantum images (FRQI) and the novel enhanced quantum representation (NEQR). Reported applications include brain tumor classification and segmentation on MRI, pneumonia detection on chest radiographs, skin and breast lesion classification, CT and PET reconstruction, and ultrasound denoising. Nearly all published systems are hybrid quantum-classical pipelines evaluated on small, downsampled benchmark datasets or simulators, and clinical deployment is not yet feasible. We conclude with current limitations and translational priorities for radiology.

item.title: From Link Availability to Deadline-Constrained Key Service: A Feasibility Framework for Mobile Free-Space Quantum Key Distribution
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it translates raw optical availability of mobile free‑space QKD links into a concrete service metric—whether time‑critical cryptographic keys can be delivered without borrowing from future contacts. By introducing a time‑indexed arrival process and a prefix‑feasibility condition, the authors give network designers a practical way to benchmark satellite, UAV or high‑altitude platform QKD against real‑world deadline constraints, complementing recent finite‑key and scheduling studies. The work shows that even a high long‑run link uptime may not guarantee usable key material for short, fragmented contacts, highlighting the importance of inventory management across acquisition windows. Readers should keep in mind that this is a systems‑level accounting framework rather than a new security proof, so its value hinges on accurate measurements of loss, noise and timing assumptions.

Mobile free-space quantum key distribution (QKD) links can provide secret bits intermittently, whereas applications may need cryptographic key material at specified times. Optical feasibility, positive finite-key output, and deadline-compliant key service are consequently different claims. This technical note formalizes their separation through a time-indexed, security-qualified arrival process and a key-inventory model. Under explicitly stated assumptions, an elementary prefix-feasibility condition characterizes whether all demands can be served without borrowing keys from future contact windows. A stylized finite block model then illustrates why positive long-run optical availability does not ensure positive finite-key output when observations are fragmented into short contacts. Two transparent numerical examples distinguish total key yield from key delivery time and show the conditional benefit of pooling data across acquisition windows. The analysis is intended as a systems-level accounting and benchmarking framework, not a new QKD security proof or a demonstration of hardware performance. It identifies measurements and security assumptions needed to evaluate train, UAV, high-altitude-platform, and satellite-assisted optical QKD against application-level service requirements.

item.title: Trace-distance characterization of recurrent pairwise synchronization in cavity-coupled superconducting qubits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a trace‑distance based metric to quantify recurrent pairwise synchronization among three cavity‑coupled superconducting qubits, offering a concrete reduced‑state tool for probing coherent collective dynamics in circuit‑QED hardware. By mapping how the synchronization window shrinks with outer‑qubit coupling and becomes insensitive to middle‑qubit strength at higher couplings, it connects directly to recent efforts to engineer robust multi‑qubit interactions and mitigate decoherence through synchronized driving. The results suggest a practical pathway for designing tunable synchronization protocols that could improve gate timing precision and error‑correlated control in near‑term quantum processors.

We theoretically investigate recurrent pairwise synchronization in three super?conducting qubits coupled to a common single-mode microwave cavity. The qubits interact indirectly through the cavity field and are driven by a coher?ent microwave field. We obtain the coherent dynamics in the dressed-state basis and quantify pairwise synchronization by the trace distance between reduced single-qubit density matrices. The trace-distance dynamics exhibit oscillatory wave-packet structures, with low-trace-distance regions identifying finite syn?chronization windows. An envelope-threshold procedure is introduced to extract the representative duration of these windows. By varying the middle-qubit coupling strength and the relative coupling ratio of the outer qubits, we con?struct a parameter-dependent map of the synchronization-window duration. The duration decreases rapidly with increasing relative outer-qubit coupling and becomes weakly dependent on the middle-qubit coupling in the stronger-coupling regime. These results provide a reduced-state-based characterization of coherent collective dynamics in multiqubit circuit-QED systems.

item.title: Classical Pre-Training of Large Shallow Parametrized Quantum Circuits through Pauli Propagation and deployment on Quantum Hardware
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a broad class of quantum‑machine‑learning models can be pre‑trained entirely on classical hardware by propagating observables backward through the circuit with Pauli propagation, sidestepping the costly parameter‑shift gradients that have limited scalability so far. By introducing weight‑ and degree‑based truncations plus pruning heuristics, the authors make the method tractable for 64‑qubit shallow ansätze and demonstrate successful deployment on IBM’s ibm_berlin processor for both a VQE Ising study and a binary‑image generative model. The result is a practical pathway to train larger quantum models with far fewer parametrized gates than IQP‑style circuits, reducing transpilation overhead and bringing near‑term quantum advantage within reach—though the approach currently relies on shallow depth and approximation choices that must be validated for deeper architectures.

Scaling parametrized quantum circuits to a larger number of qubits is a central challenge in Quantum Machine Learning: gradient estimation via the parameter-shift rule quickly becomes prohibitively expensive, while gradient-free optimizers offer limited convergence guarantees. We apply the Pauli propagation framework to a broad class of Quantum Machine Learning problems in which the loss is expressed as a function of expectation values of the circuit's observables, while keeping the relevant quantity of interest, such as the quantum state or its samples, classically intractable to compute. By propagating the observables backward through the circuit, we obtain an explicit parametric expression for the loss that can be minimized entirely on classical hardware. We also present complementary strategies to make propagation tractable at large scale, including weight-based and degree-based truncations and pruning heuristics. We demonstrate the approach on two benchmarks run on 64-qubit circuits: Variational Quantum Eigensolver on a two-dimensional Ising model, and training of a discrete-type generative model for binary images. In both cases, the classically pre-trained parameters are deployed on the IBM quantum processor ibm_berlin. For generative learning, we additionally show that the circuits considered here require substantially fewer parametrized gates than IQP-style ansätze, reducing transpilation overhead and making deployment on current quantum hardware feasible.

item.title: LYNX - A trapped-ion quantum information processor
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article showcases LYNX, a trapped‑ion processor that pushes ion‑based hardware into the same performance tier as leading superconducting systems by delivering sub‑10⁻⁴ single‑qubit errors and two‑qubit errors below 3×10⁻³ across a 24‑qubit register. The all‑to‑all connectivity and a demonstrated quantum volume of 2¹⁵ signal that trapped ions can now support deep, highly entangled circuits at scales relevant for early error‑corrected algorithms. While the QV benchmark stops at 15 qubits, the reported gate fidelities suggest LYNX is poised to accelerate both quantum‑chemistry simulations and the development of fault‑tolerant logical qubits on ion platforms.

We introduce LYNX, a quantum information processor based on trapped $^{40}$Ca$^+$ ions. It utilizes up to 31 qubits with all-to-all connectivity. We characterize the system performance using rigorous benchmarks, such as randomized benchmarking (RB), GHZ state fidelity estimates, and quantum volume (QV) tests. The LYNX processor shows average 1-qubit gate errors of $8(5)\times 10^{-5}$ tested via standard RB in a 24-qubit register. An average 2-qubit gate error in a 24-qubit register of $2.84(8)\times 10^{-3}$ is demonstrated using interleaved RB. Furthermore, the device passes QV tests using up to 15 qubits which corresponds to a quantum volume of QV$=2^{15}$.

item.title: Entangled logical qubits on a superconducting quantum processor
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks a concrete step toward fault‑tolerant quantum computing by showing that logical qubits encoded in surface codes can be created, entangled and teleported on a real superconducting processor with error rates below the 1 % threshold for each round of error correction. By combining component selection, fast reset to suppress leakage, and noise‑aware decoding, the IBM Phoenix team pushes distance‑5 surface‑code performance into a regime where logical operations begin to outpace raw physical errors—a milestone that aligns with recent advances in lattice‑surgery protocols and multi‑round stabilizer cycles reported by other groups. The demonstrated logical Bell fidelities above 93 % and teleportation of gates suggest that near‑term applications such as error‑corrected quantum sensing or small‑scale algorithmic primitives could soon be run on hardware that already incorporates the essential ingredients for scalable fault tolerance.

We demonstrate high-fidelity logical qubit operations using \texttt{ibm\_phoenix}, a square-lattice array of 120 coupled superconducting qubits that are capable of fast reset. Using strategies to exclude underperforming components together with noise informed decoding, we routinely produce surface codes at distance-3 and distance-5 with logical error per round below 1\%. We demonstrate entanglement between two logical qubits, where logical Bell-state fidelities above 93\% are observed for entanglement created via lattice surgery. With three logical qubits and lattice surgery, we perform logical teleportation of a range of states and gates, observing fidelities in the range 78\% - 93\%. Using reset to reduce qubit leakage, we show that repeated rounds of stabilizer measurements continue to exhibit improvements in a stability experiment up to $\sim 2\cdot 10^{-7}$ over 170 measurement rounds.

item.title: Finite Nonsignalling Resources Suffice to Simulate Entangled Qubits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article settles a decades‑old open problem by proving that any pure two‑qubit entangled state can be reproduced exactly with only a finite number of PR‑boxes and shared randomness, eliminating the need for continuous‑alphabet resources or communication. By giving an explicit worst‑case bound that scales modestly with the Schmidt angle, it clarifies the resource hierarchy in Bell nonlocality and shows that the apparent continuity of quantum correlations does not demand infinite‑dimensional simulators. While the construction is presently a theoretical tool rather than a hardware blueprint, it opens new avenues for efficient classical‑plus‑non‑signalling simulations of entangled systems and deepens our understanding of what underlies quantum advantage in sensing and communication protocols.

A longstanding question in Bell nonlocality is whether finite-alphabet nonsignalling resources can reproduce the continuum of measurement correlations of partially entangled qubits. Here we resolve this problem by showing that every fixed pure two-qubit state admits an exact simulation of all local projective-measurement statistics using shared randomness and finitely many Popescu-Rohrlich (PR) boxes, without communication or postselection. The boxes operate in parallel, with a worst-case bound independent of the measurement settings: at most $128\cot^4θ$ calls for the Schmidt state $\cosθ|00\rangle+\sinθ|11\rangle$, $0<θ<π/4$. The key is an exact finite-selection method that reduces input-dependent continuous sampling to a choice from a fixed-length shared random list, implemented through a finite PR-box network. The construction extends to arbitrary mixed two-qubit states and local binary-outcome POVMs. This reveals a fundamental separation between the continuity of quantum measurement correlations and the alphabet size of the resources needed to simulate them, shedding light on the resource-theoretic structure of Bell nonlocality.

item.title: Two-Layer Verification for Fault-Tolerant Magic-State Preparation in High-Rate Quantum Codes
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a long‑standing bottleneck in fault‑tolerant quantum computing by showing how to prepare high‑quality magic states directly within a compact, high‑rate code rather than relying on costly distillation pipelines. The two‑layer verification scheme—local checks on subblocks followed by a logical check after embedding—captures error patterns that ordinary parity checks miss, and the authors demonstrate distance‑5 suppression for both T and S states in a [[21,3,5]] code. By integrating magic‑state preparation into multi‑logical‑qubit encodings, the work points toward more resource‑efficient universal gates on near‑term error‑corrected devices, though its performance still hinges on low physical error rates and scalable implementation of the verification circuits.

Encoded magic states are essential for universal fault-tolerant quantum computation, but their resource-efficient preparation in high-rate quantum codes remains challenging. To address this limitation, we propose two-layer verification, which combines local verification of independently prepared subblocks with logical verification after their embedding into a target code. This hierarchy detects harmful error patterns, including even-parity logical-eigenvalue flips that are invisible to a collective product check alone. We demonstrate this scheme for a $[[21,3,5]]$ code by constructing a circuit that embeds three verified seven-qubit Steane-code magic states into the target code. Circuit-level simulations of $T$- and $S$-state preparation show logical-error suppression consistent with the code distance. These results demonstrate the potential of two-layer verification as a design principle for reliable magic-state preparation in quantum codes encoding multiple logical qubits.

item.title: Traceable Quantum Secret Sharing
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a long‑standing blind spot in quantum secret sharing by adding built‑in accountability, allowing the system to pinpoint which participant leaked or forged a share. By defining leakage‑verifiable and malicious‑traceable protocols and proving their security, it extends recent advances in distributed quantum cryptography—such as networked QKD and multiparty computation—into a more realistic threat model where insiders can be compromised. The simulations show that verification steps are the most noise‑sensitive, highlighting an engineering challenge for near‑term quantum networks but also offering a clear roadmap for implementing traceable security on future quantum internet infrastructures.

Quantum secret sharing protects distributed quantum information against unauthorized reconstruction, yet existing schemes provide no intrinsic accountability when shares are leaked or forged. This missing capability is particularly relevant in realistic distributed settings, where compromised participants may either expose valid shares or maliciously interfere with reconstruction. Here we establish a framework for traceable quantum secret sharing under these two threat models. We introduce leakage-verifiable and traceable quantum secret sharing (LVT-QSS), which attributes leaked shares through an explicit leakage verification mechanism, and malicious-traceable and accountable quantum secret sharing (MTA-QSS), which identifies participants who submit forged shares during reconstruction. We formulate security definitions for both settings and prove that the proposed protocols satisfy the corresponding guarantees against the relevant adversaries. Numerical simulations under per-share depolarizing noise further quantify the robustness of the proposed schemes and identify verification as the dominant noise sensitive stage. These results incorporate accountability into quantum secret sharing and provide a foundation for traceable distributed quantum cryptography.

item.title: Photon-Number Discrimination from Increasing Time-of-Arrival Separation in Wide Superconducting Microstrip Single-Photon Detectors
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that wide NbN superconducting microstrip single‑photon detectors can discriminate photon number up to n = 8 by exploiting increasingly separated time‑of‑arrival peaks, achieving a pairwise assignment fidelity of 99.6 %—a stark contrast to the compressed timing shifts seen in conventional narrow‑wire SNSPDs. By turning timing information into a reliable photon‑number readout, the work offers a hardware‑efficient alternative to multiplexed or transition‑edge sensor approaches, potentially simplifying multiphoton state tomography and photonic quantum‑information protocols. It builds on recent advances in SNSPD speed and efficiency, but the technique’s performance still depends on maintaining low jitter at lower photon numbers and on precise microstrip geometry. Readers should care because scalable, high‑fidelity number resolution is a key bottleneck for many optical quantum computing applications.

Measurements of photon-number-dependent time-of-arrival (TOA) distributions in wide NbN superconducting microstrip single-photon detectors (SMSPDs) are presented. Two \SI{10}{\um}-long devices with widths of \SI{3.2}{\um} and \SI{6.4}{\um} are characterized under pulsed \SI{515}{nm} excitation. The TOA histograms are described by sums of exponentially modified Gaussian (EMG) components, with the wider device exhibiting components assigned to photon numbers up to \(n=8\). Adjacent TOA peaks become more distinguishable relative to their widths at higher photon number, in contrast to the compression of neighboring photon-number timing shifts observed in conventional narrow-wire SNSPDs. For the components assigned to \(n=7\) and \(n=8\), the FWHM-normalized peak separation is \(2.15\), and the fitted EMG distributions yield an equal-prior pairwise TOA-assignment fidelity of \(99.6\%\). The EMG exponential-tail parameter \(τ_n\) decreases strongly with photon number, while the Gaussian-location parameter \(μ_n\) continues to shift between neighboring components. A phenomenological model motivated by absorption-site-dependent vortex processes and collective current redistribution captures these timing trends. These results support wide SMSPDs as a platform for TOA-based photon-number discrimination at high photon number, relevant to multiphoton-state characterization and photonic quantum information processing. The same geometry also provides a setting to examine how the spatial distribution of photon absorption affects vortex-assisted detection.

item.title: Trident: Efficient Load Verification for Yoked Surface Codes using a Three-Level Memory Hierarchy
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces Trident, a three‑level memory hierarchy that inserts a fast, low‑overhead 1D yoked surface code tier between the compute‑focused surface code and the high‑density 2D YSC storage layer, cutting the costly verification step that currently dominates load latency. By leveraging the negligible verification time of 1D YSCs, Trident can reduce memory‑access delays by up to 5.7× while preserving the 4.5× storage efficiency advantage of 2D YSCs—an advance that directly tackles one of the biggest practical bottlenecks in fault‑tolerant architectures. If hardware designs can accommodate the extra tier, the approach could make large‑scale quantum programs far more responsive and bring hierarchical error‑correction schemes closer to deployment.

Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computers (FTQCs) commonly use the surface code to encode program qubits as error-corrected logical qubits. Unfortunately, the surface code has a poor encoding rate, so recent work has proposed Yoked Surface Codes (YSCs), which concatenate the surface code with a high-rate quantum code. The surface code qubits in YSCs are protected by the checks, or yokes, of the high-rate code. YSCs have 1D and 2D variants, which are $1.8\times$ and $4.5\times$ more efficient than the surface code, respectively. Modern FTQC architectures use a two-level hierarchy: surface codes perform logical operations (compute) while 2D YSCs store idle program qubits (memory). To load a qubit from memory, the FTQC first performs retrieval, which logically moves a program qubit from a 2D YSC into a surface code (8 cycles). However, retrieval is not fault-tolerant, so the FTQC must verify the load by measuring all the yokes of the 2D YSC (178 cycles). As verification dominates memory access latency, eliminating it can provide a speedup of $5.7\times$. Our goal is to reduce the verification overhead of 2D YSCs while retaining their storage efficiency. We exploit the fact that 1D YSCs, though less storage-efficient, incur negligible verification latency. We propose Trident, which expands the two-level hierarchy into a three-level hierarchy by adding a small intermediate level containing a 1D YSC (L1). If most loads hit L1 rather than L2 (2D YSC tier), it can significantly reduce verification overhead. We present two variants: Trident-D (demand-driven) and Trident-P (prefetch-driven), which achieve speedups of $2.8\times$ and $4.2\times$, respectively, while increasing the physical qubit cost of memory by only 4.9%.

item.title: Screening strongly correlated materials in solid oxide cells with quantum simulation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how a full‑stack quantum workflow could tackle the notoriously hard problem of screening strongly correlated oxygen‑electrode materials for solid‑oxide fuel and electrolysis cells, moving beyond classical density‑functional tricks to quantum impurity solvers that deliver finite‑temperature Green’s functions. By embedding GW‑based methods such as GW+DMFT or SEET within a quantum simulation of the active space, the authors outline a concrete path toward quantum advantage in predicting vacancy formation energies and migration barriers—key metrics for electrolyte‑electrode performance. If the projected qubit counts and thermal‑state preparation costs can be met with near‑term error‑corrected hardware, the approach could dramatically shorten materials discovery cycles for high‑efficiency energy conversion devices.

We develop an end-to-end framework for assessing a quantum-computing application in industrial materials science: the screening of strongly correlated oxygen-electrode materials for SOFCs and SOECs. We formulate the materials problem in terms of interface observables including oxygen-vacancy formation energies, vacancy migration barriers, and electronic conductivity. We describe how these observables can be obtained using a diagrammatic GW-based embedding, either GW+DMFT or self-energy embedding theory (SEET), applied to a DFT-screened shortlist. The atomistic electrode/electrolyte interface defines the electronic structure problem from which the correlated impurity models are constructed. Quantum impurity solvers would provide the finite-temperature impurity Green's functions required by the embedding. The computational challenges that classical solvers may encounter as the interacting active space grows, together with the polynomial scaling of quantum Hamiltonian simulation for efficiently represented discretized models, open an opportunity for quantum advantage. We identify the benchmarks needed to assess this opportunity through convergence of vacancy and migration energetics and comparison with the best applicable classical solvers. We provide illustrative logical qubit counts and identify the thermal state preparation, simulation, measurement, and repeated-solve costs needed for a complete resource assessment. We connect microscopic observables to macroscopic engineering metrics using a continuum model for mixed ionic--electronic conducting oxygen electrodes that couples oxygen surface exchange, solid-state oxygen transport, electrode microstructure, and finite electrode thickness. Finally, we estimate the potential worldwide business value of improved electrode materials under SOFC and SOEC deployment scenarios informed by public technical targets and electrolyser deployment data.

item.title: Problem-aware sampling for bias and variance reduction in randomised Hamiltonian simulation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces StateDRIFT, a problem‑aware twist on the popular qDRIFT randomised simulation technique that tailors its sampling distribution using information about the initial state and observable of interest, thereby cutting both bias and variance. By solving a modest optimisation at each Trotter step, the authors demonstrate order‑of‑magnitude reductions in two‑qubit gate counts for realistic molecular dynamics (e.g., BeH₂ drops from ~11 k to under 1 k gates), a gain that could make high‑fidelity Hamiltonian simulation feasible on near‑term devices. The approach does rely on auxiliary classical estimates—via tensor‑network surrogates or classical shadows—but the reported savings suggest a practical pathway for integrating smarter sampling into quantum‑simulation pipelines.

Randomised quantum simulation algorithms such as qDRIFT reduce circuit depth by replacing deterministic product formulas with stochastic compilations, but achieving high accuracy can require many steps. In vanilla qDRIFT, Hamiltonian terms are sampled with probabilities proportional to their coefficient magnitudes. We propose StateDRIFT, a variant of qDRIFT which optimises its sampling distribution to estimate time-evolved quantities using knowledge of the initial state and target observable, with a provable truncation bound that keeps qDRIFT's guarantees. The distribution at each depth is chosen by solving an optimisation problem targeting bias and/or variance. StateDRIFT can significantly reduce the bias and variance of estimators, and hence circuit depth, which we test on short-time dynamics of lattice models and molecules under Jordan-Wigner up to 18 qubits. For example, with BeH2 StateDRIFT can reduce the number of two-qubit gates required to achieve a given accuracy from 11,201 to 983. StateDRIFT involves measuring observables and commutators on the initial state, so we propose two practical ways to estimate these: classical surrogates such as tensor networks, and classical shadows, which recover most or all of the saving from exact oracles in the systems tested.

item.title: Qubits Are Not Enough: Deflation and Measurement Limits in Variational Quantum Modal Analysis
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that simply adding more qubits does not automatically yield better modal analyses; it rigorously refines the deflation condition for variational quantum eigensolvers and quantifies how approximate projectors and Pauli‑term growth limit accuracy in realistic finite‑element problems. By mapping a generalized eigenproblem to a mass‑orthonormal Hamiltonian via Cholesky whitening, the authors expose a concrete resource bottleneck—an order‑of‑magnitude increase in operator density—that explains why current VQE implementations still lag classical methods despite modest qubit counts. The study therefore provides a valuable benchmark for algorithm‑hardware co‑design and cautions practitioners that any quantum speedup in structural dynamics will require more than just larger registers, highlighting the need for smarter encodings and error mitigation strategies.

Amplitude encoding stores an N-degree-of-freedom structural mode using ceiling(log2 N) qubits. This article develops an evaluation framework for variational quantum eigensolvers in finite-element structural dynamics. A Cholesky transformation maps the generalized eigenproblem to a symmetric mass-orthonormal Hamiltonian, ensuring Euclidean quantum-state orthogonality equals structural mass orthogonality. For higher modes, the deflation penalty condition is sharpened to a necessary-and-sufficient threshold, with a Davis-Kahan bound quantifying effects of approximate projectors. Numerical studies separate mapping correctness, ansatz expressibility, preprocessing, Pauli growth, finite-shot uncertainty, and damage localization. For 128-DOF chains, consistent-mass whitening increases transformed-operator density from 0.023 to 0.308 and Pauli terms from 576 to 2950. Exact state-vector experiments show qubit count and circuit expressibility are distinct. At 10^5 shots per Pauli term, first-mode frequency RMS error is 2.45%. In an oracle-state study, 10% stiffness loss is localized in 84.5% of trials. Results sharpen the deflation condition, quantify resource bottlenecks, and claim no speedup.

item.title: Automating quantum circuit optimization with AI agents
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that AI‑driven agents can automatically discover and certify quantum circuit optimizations, turning a traditionally manual, heuristic process into a reproducible, verifiable workflow. By integrating an exact verifier built through the same autonomous loop, the method achieves up to 73 % reductions in gate counts for key compilation tasks such as fermion‑to‑qubit encoding, Hamiltonian layout and unitary synthesis—outperforming existing hand‑tuned and state‑of‑the‑art tools. If these AI agents scale to larger problem instances, they could dramatically shorten the compile‑time bottleneck that currently limits the deployment of sophisticated algorithms on near‑term quantum hardware.

Compiling quantum algorithms for real devices involves hard optimization problems that can decide whether an algorithm runs at scale. We present a general method for solving such problems with AI agents, with every result certified. It builds on autoresearch loops, in which agents iteratively improve programs against a fixed evaluator and which have recently improved quantum cryptanalysis circuits, and adds two elements: a frozen, exact verifier certifies every result, and this verifier, together with the challenge around it, is built by an agent that formulates the problem with a researcher and validates the verifier against a solved case, deliberately broken solutions and published results before any solution exists. The method applies to any optimization problem whose solutions can be verified exactly and efficiently. We apply it to three compilation problems in quantum simulation, namely fermion-to-qubit encoding, Hamiltonian layout and unitary synthesis. In each, the agents improved substantially on published or standard constructions, reducing the cost being optimized by up to 73% at the largest sizes tested and outperforming a state-of-the-art optimizer for fermion-to-qubit encodings. Every submission is a program accompanied by its agent's notes, so the ideas behind each improvement are recorded in human-readable form; later agents built on them, and we describe them here. These results open the way to automated, certified discovery across quantum circuit design and beyond.
